[b]EXCERPT FROM: Curiosity Textbooks: Lavian History and Geopolitical Relations[/b]
-----------------------------------------------------
[i][b]Lavian Geopolitics in the 1880s, Shamat:
Lavinsworths Interest in West Shamat[/b][/i]
In the 1880s, Sir Lavinsworth took a special interest in West Shamat. In 1879, maritime traders from West Shamat caught his eye during a regular inspection trip to naval forts in Northern Rarari. Some soldiers at Fort Tabern decided to buy goods such as multicolored linen blankets from Shamati traders, who only visited the area due to it having the most northeastern port on the island. The soldiers preferred the blankets to the standard issue cotton blankets of the army due to the materials moisture-wicking properties, helping them keep cool in the humid summers and warm in the winters. Sir Lavinsworth took note of this, and after the inspection of the fort decided to venture out to the local market to find these traders.

The trip to the fort had a profound change on Sir Lavinsworth. Advisers would write that much of his free time was now dedicated to sharing his interest with his family and close friends, as well as sending trusted people to go north and bring him back items from the port. In nine months, he had acquired various blankets, rugs, a saber, and multiple hide shields, along with eating many foods imported from Shamat. Eventually, Kavavenga, the king of Swabati, a small collection of islands on the southwest coast of West Shamat, heard news of the special interest of Sir Lavinsworth and sent envoys to travel to the island of Rarari to meet with him. Once the news of the envoys arriving reached Sir Lavinsworth, he rushed to board a train and travel to meet them. After greeting them, the procession traveled to the nearby customs house and began talks from there. The envoys presented goods such as bundles of linen, Swabati wine, and a specially made banner that showed the flag of Greater Lavia and the newly created flag of Swabati. Delighted by the items, Sir Lavinsworth made plans to accompany the envoys on their return trip, bringing his own gifts.

Organizing a small fleet of two cutters and the steam cutter Theadoran, the ships were loaded with cargo such as Te-Gra Model-6 rifles, PA Model-1 revolvers, a large grandfather clock, and other curiosities and amenities that Sir Lavinsworths aids noticed that the envoys marveled at, as well as multiple preserved foods and 10 barrels of various alcohol. Sailing across the ocean, the convoy was never harassed due to the firepower of the Theadoran and a deal the previous king of Swabati made with most pirate kingdoms. Once landed and offloaded, the gifts were presented to King Kavavenga, who was as elated as Sir Lavinsworth was. Both kings proceeded to go on a week-long tour of Sawbatis capital island, and in this time made many deals, one of them being a defensive alliance focused on rebellion. After this tour, Sir Lavinsworth established an embassy near King Kavavengas palace and returned to Greater Lavia, although both frequently communicated through letters and hired messengers.

[i][b]Invasion of the Witulo Empire[/b][/i]
After the excursion to Swabati, Sir Lavinswoths interest in Western Shamat was satisfied to an extent, but it would seek him out once again, this time in a war. The Witulo Empire (near modern-day Spanish lands), was a piracy-based kingdom. Deploying privateers to the sea, the nation would gain income by its forces raiding supply routes and occasionally raiding coastal towns, as well as imposing hefty protection fees upon other nations in addition to using its flag to safely export goods. In 1883, the empire decided to up its raiding of trade routes and expand its raiding to the trade routes between Swabati and Greater Lavia due to decreased success of their older raiding routes.

At this time, Greater Lavia was focusing on greatly expanding its fleet. With the addition of 11 steamships (one battleship, 3 frigates, 3 corvettes, and 4 sloops-o-war) and one Spinell-class ironclad in 1882 alone. The combination of this new threat that threatened a diplomatically important route and the newly expanded Lavian navy created a powderkeg. For two months, Lavian and Swabati ships patrolled the route, many noting sightings of Witulo privateers shadowing their movements and observing. On May 17th, 1883, the powderkeg sparked. Two Witulo privateer ships captured and looted a Lavian merchant vessel, as well as executing its captain. In response to this, Sir Lavinsworth organized a fleet of 26 warships, eight troop transports, and with the addition of nine Swabati ships under the command of Rahbin Dinde, the fleet set out towards Witulo.

Wituli privateers would harass the fleet as they sailed north, however only wounding one sailor. Once they reached the south of Witulo, the fleet off-boarded their troops. One ironclad was dispatched along with 7 other ships to sail to the capitol and request a negotiator, while the deployed troops and other ships would advance on towns and bombard enemy positions if needed. The army first reached the small coastal town of Evimax, only facing token resistance from some police forces armed with antiquated muskets and pistols. The town was occupied, with plans for the troops to survive off of their rations or pay for what they needed as it was thought the Wituli government would surrender immediately upon the sight of the deployed ships to their capitol.

Contrary to the planning of the alliance forces, the Wituli government didnt surrender and refused to negotiate at all, rallying its forces in the north. With the return of the task force and subsequent news that there would be no negotiations, the coalition army began marching north, advancing 20 miles and digging in near the town of Madira, as well as occupying the small port located in Evimax and transforming it into a port capable of servicing the nearby fleet and receiving shipments of supplies and building materials. A week later, Wituli forces arrived in the south. Multiple small offences were launched against the alliance forces, mostly being small attacks or clashes between scouts. On June 5th, Lavian forces launched a large offencive, first seeing Watuli forces at the small, fortified town of Dumas. The Battle of Dumas lasted only a day due to the modernized state of the Lavian army, naval bombardments, and a tightening noose on their retreat route by Swabati jungle fighters employing guerrilla tactics to deprive the Watuli forces of food. Suffering ~740 casualties while only inflicting 68, Watuli forces withdrew with the exception of small groups of resistance composed of those who couldnt escape the encirclement, however these were quickly destroyed or convinced to surrender.

With the battles of Tanquey and Garta falling in much the same fashion, the underequipped and dated army of Watuli was in dire straits. Desertions were common at this point in the war among Watuli forces, further worsened by the fleeing of many government privateers to other nations. With the army crumbling and the navy now almost nonexistent after the Battle of Gifica port, alliance forces finally marched on the Watuli capital on August 23rd, 1883. Greater Lavia demanded a official surrender, but due to the robbery and subsequent murder of the Watuli royal family after their royal guards mutinied and decided to loot the palace then flee the country before alliance forces reached the capitol, the peace deal signed upon the Theadoran was signed by the Watuli royal finance minister. In this peace deal, Greater Lavia annexed almost all land of the Kingdom of Watulo, including the distant island of Tesaroso (owned entirely by the royal family itself) with some ports given to the Kingdom of Swabati, along with financial compensation for Swabatis involvement in the war, which included almost all remaining former Watuli royal possessions.
[/spoiler]
